sections.html:
Cottonwood Heights is on the east bench of the Salt Lake Valley in Salt Lake County, south of Holladay and Murray, east of Midvale and north of Sandy. It covers 9.23 square miles at about 4,820 feet. Interstate 215 runs along the northern border, and State Routes 190 and 210 lead to the canyon mouths near the eastern edge.

Big Cottonwood Canyon leads to Solitude and Brighton, and Little Cottonwood Canyon leads to Snowbird and Alta, so winter traffic on the canyon roads is part of daily life. A street near the canyon mouths feels very different from one near I-215, and buyers notice.

The city estimates 32,265 residents for July 2025, in 12,762 households and 13,536 housing units with 5.7 percent vacant. The median age is 39.1 and about 18.4 percent of residents are 65 or older, which fits a city where many owners have stayed in the same house for a long time.

Annual precipitation is about 25.9 inches, with April the wettest month at 3.49 inches and July the driest at 0.92 inches. Lots near the canyon mouths can see snowmelt run toward foundations in spring, so buyers look at grading, window wells and sump pumps near the creeks. Steeper streets often have retaining walls that age and lean.

  • Spring runoff near Big and Little Cottonwood creeks
  • Window wells and basement drainage
  • Retaining walls and sloped driveways
  • Roof and gutter wear after heavy snow

The Wasatch Fault runs along the mountain front, and the Utah Division of Emergency Management points to older unreinforced masonry as the biggest concern. Strapping a water heater and checking chimneys are simple steps before a sale.

The city office at 2277 Bengal Boulevard handles planning, zoning, building permits and inspections. The main number is 801-944-7000, and code enforcement sits under the police department.

Short-term rentals need a city license and are allowed mainly in multi-family residential areas, within condominium or homeowners association communities. If your unit has been used that way, confirm the license status before you sell.

  • Building permits: check that finished basements, decks and additions were permitted.
  • Accessory dwelling units: the city has its own ADU rules.
  • Short-term rentals: allowed only in approved areas.
  • Landscaping: the city has ordinances for outdoor lighting, trees and park strips.

Unpermitted work does not stop a cash sale, though it can stop a financed one. Sorting out which work has permits saves time if you plan to list with an agent.

sections.h2: Salt Lake County tax dates and the primary residence reduction
sections.html:
Salt Lake County bills Cottonwood Heights property tax, and the last day to pay without penalty is November 30.

Salt Lake County tax calendar
DateWhat happens
July 22Notices of Valuation mailed
November 1Tax notices mailed
November 30Last day to pay without penalty
December 1Unpaid taxes become delinquent
January 31Penalty rises from 1 percent to 2.5 percent
Fourth Thursday of MayFinal tax sale

A primary home gets a 45 percent reduction if it is occupied at least 183 consecutive days in a year. Vacation rentals, second homes and cabins do not qualify. Owners whose mailing address differs from the property address get a letter and have 30 days to file the declaration, or the reduction is removed. The declaration also creates a presumption of Utah residency for income tax purposes, so speak with a tax professional if that matters to you.

sections.h2: Timing a sale around the tax calendar
sections.html:
The tax calendar affects when you close. A house that sells between November and January sits close to the November 30 deadline and the December 1 delinquency date, so confirm with the title company whether the current year has been paid. After January 31 the penalty climbs, and the final tax sale falls on the fourth Thursday of May, so a balance that has been open a long time needs attention well before then.

If you received a letter about the primary residence declaration, answer it within the 30 days. Losing the reduction raises the bill, and a buyer who takes over a house with a removed reduction will notice the difference. Mention the status in your first conversation so it is handled on both sides.

Walk the property the way an inspector would. Check the window wells and sump pump near the creeks, look at the retaining walls on a slope, and note the age of the roof, gutters and water heater. Write down which additions have permits and which do not, and keep any permit paperwork in one place. A short written list of what you know is more useful than a guess, and it keeps a buyer from finding surprises later.

A cash sale lets you close on your own schedule, without staging, showings or repair negotiations. Here is how it runs for a Cottonwood Heights house.

  1. You describe the house, including permit questions, drainage history and any tenants.
  2. You receive an offer and decide whether to take it.
  3. A title company searches the record and requests any payoffs.
  4. You sign at a date you pick, and the unpaid tax balance, if any, is paid from your proceeds.

Have the latest county tax notice, permit records for any finished basement or addition, and short-term rental license paperwork if the unit was used that way.

Sellers here are often long-time owners, heirs or landlords with a house that needs updating. With nearly one in five residents aged 65 or older, many sales follow a change in circumstances: downsizing, a move or the loss of a family member.

  • Long-held homes with original systems that buyers want updated
  • Hillside or canyon-side lots with drainage questions
  • Estates where heirs live out of state
  • Rentals or former short-term rentals with permit or license questions

Houses with a long-time owner may also hold decades of belongings, and clearing them takes more time than most people expect. Set a move-out date early.

Estates take the most coordination. Every heir who must sign needs to be identified early, and the title company will want the paperwork that shows who has authority to sell. Starting that conversation before you ask for an offer shortens the timeline.

sections.h2: Working with local employers and buyers
sections.html: Several corporate offices sit inside city limits, including Instructure, Dyno Nobel, Extra Space Storage, Breeze Airways and JetBlue, which is unusual for a suburb. Many residents still commute across the valley. Salt Lake City International Airport is the county's only airport with scheduled passenger service, and TRAX light rail and FrontRunner serve other parts of the county. City Hall has a business development specialist who can answer questions if you own a property used for work.

faqs.q: What county is Cottonwood Heights in?
faqs.a: Salt Lake County, whose treasurer bills the property tax. Valuation notices go out around July 22 and payment is due November 30.

faqs.q: Where do I check which school district serves my address?
faqs.a: The Canyons School District serves Cottonwood Heights, and its School Finder tool checks boundaries by address. Buyers often use it before making an offer.

faqs.q: Are short-term rentals allowed in Cottonwood Heights?
faqs.a: They need a city license and are allowed mainly in multi-family residential areas within condominium or HOA communities. Ask city staff whether a specific property is eligible.

faqs.q: How does the primary residence reduction work in Salt Lake County?
faqs.a: A primary residence occupied at least 183 consecutive days in a year gets a 45 percent reduction in taxable value. Vacation homes and second homes do not qualify.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Cottonwood Heights house with unpermitted work?
faqs.a: Yes, it can be sold as it is. Tell the buyer what was done, since permit status can affect financing and later inspections.
